extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology and media/journalism studies; researchers interested in news production theory
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying theoretical criteria about how news is produced, framed, and functions as social knowledge; focuses on interpretive sociological concepts (Schutz, Garfinkel, Goffman, Berger & Luckmann) as applied to newswork. Useful for analyzing newsworthiness, framing, institutional constraints, and ideology in news production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional sociological view: news mirrors social structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Society's social structure produces norms and attitudes that define what is of interest or importance; newsworkers, socialized to those societal attitudes and professional norms, cover and disseminate items identified as interesting or important so that news presents a mirror of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that for definitions of news to change, the social structure and institutions must change first; example: Roshco (1975) and the 'man bites dog' prototype of soft news leading to social change only if widely adopted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach: news as active construction by newsworkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers and news organizations actively invoke and apply norms to define newsworthiness moment-to-moment; news does not simply mirror society but helps constitute social phenomena by defining and shaping events as they report them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes negotiation among news actors (e.g., editors deciding page-one items); examples include news construing early women's movement as 'ridiculous bra burners'—the press imposes meanings that define deviance and normativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schutz: natural attitude (taken-for-grantedness of social phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Social actors accept social phenomena (including news) as objective givens rather than bracketing them; the everyday world is constituted by this taken-for-granted stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schutz's six classic characteristics of the natural attitude: (1) wide-awakedness (attention to life), (2) suspension of doubt (epoché), (3) working spontaneity (project-oriented action), (4) the working self as total self, (5) common intersubjective world, (6) a standard time-perspective; readers accept 'news' and 'today's news' as given and work to apprehend meaning from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethnomethodological invariants: reflexivity and indexicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflexivity: accounts are embedded in the reality they describe and in producing them people reproduce social arrangements. Indexicality: meanings of accounts depend on the context of production and can be reattributed when removed from that context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These twin concepts explain how utterances and news reports gain meaning contextually and how severing context (indexical attribution) transforms them; examples: the conversational 'uh' is meaningless without context; naming 'the day Joe said x' as an indexical particular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public character of news: selective abstraction and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: News provides a selective abstraction of events designed to be coherent for audiences while omitting many details; consumers then add details (not necessarily those omitted by reporters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by My Lai and Watergate: until selective accounts were disseminated, these occurrences had limited public existence. Selective abstraction turns private troubles into public issues and is integral to news's public character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification of facts: presenting facts divorced from production context
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters may quote sources or state facts without indicating how those statements or facts were produced, thereby objectifying them as nonproblematic particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This indexical presentation produces ahistoricity and a 'logic of the concrete'—a refusal to situate events historically or in ongoing context. Examples noted: quoting without revealing the prompt (see p.96) and identifying facts without explaining their production (see p.88).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame analysis (Goffman): frames organize events and impart character
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame is the principle of organization governing events and subjective involvement; a 'strip' is an arbitrary slice of ongoing activity. Frames make happenings recognizable as events and give them social meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames both transform occurrences into events and events into news stories; example provided of the editor-reporter exchange about a fire and 'six graphs'—the frame makes the fire 'a minor fire worth six paragraphs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary framing limits information and thus creates meaning (be skeptical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary framing relies on limiting information about the interconnectedness of literal events; by imposing order and leaving out context, documentary frames necessarily create particular meanings and portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goffman warns that documentary forms can be suspect relative to standards of documentation; camera shots and sequencing on television frame spatial and relational meanings and should be scrutinized for imposed meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newswork embedded in territorial, institutional, and topical chains (the 'news net')
rubrics_metrics.description: News production is enmeshed in organizational structures—territorial, institutional, and topical chains of responsibility—that require ongoing negotiation and shape what becomes news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ties to earlier chapters: the news net anchors reporters to legitimated institutions and requires negotiation among competitor-colleagues; this embeddedness shapes selection, sourcing, and presentation of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal typifications and the rhythm of work shape news selection
rubrics_metrics.description: News is temporally grounded: typifications rooted in the rhythm of work (what is 'today's news') determine attention, selection, and the timeframe within which occurrences are apprehended as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The socially defined time frame (intersection of human experience and celestial cycles as Schutz puts it) structures how readers and newsworkers apprehend stories; temporal grounding contributes to ahistoricity and the logic of the concrete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual constitution of facts and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and sources are co-produced: newsworkers' understandings of institutions and political processes shape which actors are treated as authoritative sources and which facts are surfaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: identifying municipal government as 'the city' or designating Betty Friedan a 'responsible spokesperson'—these transformations rely on reporters' methods and institutional understandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional objectification: procedures become 'the way to do things' and constrain innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social interactions produce meanings that become institutionalized as rules and procedures; removed from original contexts, these procedures appear as objective, handed-down ways of doing things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to common-sense assumptions about news (e.g., news is ahistorical, centralized, embedded in legitimated institutions) and can impede the emergence of new forms of news so long as processing remains tied to those institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology as objectified 'interested procedures' (Smith): procedures as means of not knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures embedded in legitimated institutions (indexical, reflexive, objectified, framing practices) function as 'interested procedures'—methods that produce social structures while truncating actors' ability to transform those institutions and that serve as means of not knowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith's critique locates ideology in institutionalized procedures that present a limited knowledge regime; applies both to newswork (how news reproduces institutions) and to social science practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexicality/ahistoricity risk: researchers treating news as veridical event data
rubrics_metrics.description: Because news can be indexically presented and objectified, social scientists may mistakenly use news reports as if they were accurate depictions of occurrences rather than accounts produced within specific production contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warnings citing Danzger and Tuchman: using news as raw data without reference to production context risks conflating the news story with the event itself and misinterpreting the nature of social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame-seeking and negotiation as routine newswork
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors actively search for and negotiate frames that will make occurrences fit editorial space and institutional conventions; finding an appropriate frame is central to getting a story published or broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Van Gelder seeking a frame for a women's demonstration story; Seaboard City Daily seeking a frame to state no heat in a tenement; television uses camera shots as framing devices—frames are negotiated phenomena.
